title: Branches Are Movable Labels, Not Copies

questions.prompt: You create a branch and immediately switch to it. What actually happened on disk?
options: The whole project was duplicated into a new directory
A file under .git/refs/heads was written containing one commit hash, and HEAD was pointed at it
A second copy of every object was added to .git/objects
Nothing on disk changed until the first commit on the new branch
questions.explanation: A branch is one file holding one hash, so creation and switching are both instant metadata edits — which is why creating twenty branches costs nothing. A directory copy (A) and a second object store (B) are both the copy mental model this lesson removes. Option D is wrong in the same direction: HEAD is moved at switch time, before any commit exists on the branch.

questions.prompt: A branch holds three commits nobody else has. You run git branch -D on it. Which statement is true?
options: The three commits are deleted immediately and are unrecoverable
The commits remain in the object store and are reachable through the reflog, but nothing references them as a branch any more
The three commits are moved onto whichever branch you are currently on
The delete fails because unmerged commits cannot be removed under any flag
questions.explanation: -D removes the label, not the commits. They stay reachable via reflog for now; garbage collection is what eventually reclaims them, so 'recoverable' is a matter of timing, not certainty. Immediate destruction (A) overstates it — that is what garbage collection does later. Nothing re-parents your commits onto your current branch (C); that is what merge and rebase do, explicitly. And -D exists precisely to override the safety refusal (D), which is why plain -d refusing is meaningful.

questions.prompt: A colleague runs git checkout main -- config.json, expecting to switch branches, and the working tree changes under them instead. Why is this confusing rather than a git bug?
options: It is a known bug fixed in recent git versions
checkout does two unrelated jobs — moving between branches and restoring files — and only the second one is a real file restore
They were in detached HEAD, so checkout ignored the branch argument
questions.explanation: checkout carries two meanings, and `--` plus a path selects the file-restoring one. Nothing is broken (A) and the separator is valid syntax (C). Detached HEAD (D) has nothing to do with it — the file restore happens regardless of what HEAD points at. This is exactly why the lesson recommends `switch` for branch moves and `restore` for files: split commands so the argument shape tells you which job you are doing.

questions.prompt: You are in detached HEAD after checking out a commit to inspect it. You make a commit here and switch away. How would you find that commit a week later?
options: git branch — it will show up as a detached entry you can check out
git log, which lists commits with no branch by default
git reflog, which records every HEAD move including the ones made while detached
There is no way; commits outside a branch are not retained
questions.explanation: The reflog is a local record of where HEAD has pointed, and it includes detached positions — that is the whole reason it is the answer to 'where was that?'. `git branch` (A) lists labels, and there is no label here, which is the whole difficulty. `git log` (B) follows refs, so it will not volunteer your orphaned commit. And they are retained (D) — but only because of the reflog, which is a weaker guarantee than having a named branch.
